idiom_name: poll(2)/select(2) timeout loop or POSIX mq_timedreceive
implementation_notes: C has no consumer abstraction, so the pattern is a hand-written loop over transport primitives: poll()/select() with a millisecond timeout - a 0 return is the idle tick, -1 with EINTR is a signal (retry, not failure) - or mq_timedreceive() with an absolute timespec deadline for POSIX message queues. The consumer owns everything the pattern assigns to it: the idle interval and its backoff, how many descriptors or messages are drained per wake-up, and acknowledgement (removal from the queue is the ack; on a byte-stream channel the offset must be tracked by the application).
pitfalls: poll() returning 0 is the idle tick and -1 with EINTR is an interrupted wait; treating either as a broken channel makes an idle consumer look dead or makes it drop wake-ups.
A zero or forgotten timeout turns the loop into a busy-wait that burns a core; with many channels one thread should demultiplex via epoll/select instead of running one polling thread per descriptor.
Reading a byte stream gives no message boundaries and removal is not an acknowledgement, so without an explicit offset or ack store a crash after read() loses the message silently.
